Introduced a new OCR-based receipt scanning module from scratch.

Project overview

A new module for the Placewise loyalty app — members scan store receipts to earn points. Covers the full end-to-end flow: mobile scanning, OCR processing, data review, and a back-office verification panel for mall managers.

From requirements and OCR evaluation through UX flows for two user groups, UAT, and launch. A technically complex project with a high degree of interdependencies between user journeys.

01 — Understanding

Product
Definition

A new sellable module for Placewise clients. Members scan store receipts to earn loyalty points — on mobile app and webforms. Mall managers verify flagged scans in MPC back-office.

Before this project, users had no way to submit receipts digitally — the feature was introduced from scratch. First step: align with PMs on scope, map OCR constraints with ML engineers, define the boundary between automated and manual verification.

Business goal
New revenue module

Sellable add-on for shopping centres — spend-based point rewards to increase member engagement.

Two user groups
Members + managers
  • Members scanning via mobile app or webform
  • Mall managers verifying flagged scans in MPC
Key constraint
OCR accuracy limits

OCR reliably reads store name, date, total amount. Human verification unavoidable for edge cases.

02 — Research

Insights

Research ran in parallel with technical exploration. On the design side, I benchmarked existing loyalty apps with receipt scanning from different sectors. Alongside this, extensive discussions with the ML team covered technical capabilities and constraints.

Research showed that users needed clear validation and review steps to trust OCR-generated data — which directly shaped the correction flow and manual verification panel.

Other loyalty apps
Key benchmark patterns
  • Multi-step form with clear instructions before upload
  • Key pattern: showing users exactly what must be visible on the receipt before they scan
  • Status transparency — users need immediate, clear feedback on scan outcome
  • Ambiguous "waiting" states lead to duplicate submissions and frustration
ML team collaboration
Technical requirements & constraints
  • What data can reliably be extracted: store name, date, total amount
  • How extracted data matches against the store database — and what's missing (store addresses needed for verification)
  • Which error types need to be handled by the design
  • Fraud prevention methods and their UX implications
Design implication
Loading state is unavoidable

OCR takes time. Clear scanning state needed so users don't assume failure and resubmit.

Design implication
Always allow correction

OCR is best-effort. Members must review and edit extracted data before submitting.

Design implication
Fraud prevention = UX

9 high-priority user stories defined. Duplicate detection and time-based rejection were core requirements, not edge cases.

03 — Analysis

Two flows.
Mapped.

Two parallel user journeys — member scanning flow and manager verification flow — with significant interdependencies. The biggest design challenge: handling three interconnected aspects simultaneously — the end user perspective, the manager perspective, and the limit/rule system that affects both.

The main design tension was balancing OCR automation with enough user control to catch and correct errors.

Member journey
Scan → confirm → result
  • 3-step onboarding before first scan (revisitable) — rules, what to photograph, benefits
  • Camera permission flow handled within app
  • Scanner tab: photo or file upload
  • Large number of edge cases and error states designed from the start — unreadable receipt, limit exceeded, wrong store, duplicate, too old
  • History view: Approved / Waiting / Rejected with reason
Manager journey (MPC)
Verify → approve or reject
  • Default view: receipts awaiting manual verification
  • Verification reason immediately visible — no guessing
  • Duplicate review: side-by-side comparison before decision
  • Mandatory confirmation to prevent accidental approval/rejection
  • Full scan history per member

Screens
delivered.

Design split into stages — the MPC admin panel first, then the end user UI. In practice, this required switching between both frequently due to the strong interdependencies. High degree of complexity, but high satisfaction with the final result.

End user — Mobile App screens

Designed for fast submission, but with clear checkpoints for review and correction — onboarding, scan confirmation, OCR validation, and result states all exist to prevent errors before they reach the manager.

05 — Testing

QA &
iterations.

QA testing carried out on a collection of real receipts — searching for errors caused by illegibility, grease marks, or damage (a surprisingly common case 😄). Verification with clients and the sales team. Bug fixing and design corrections.

UAT and QA feedback helped catch edge cases early and prevented production issues.

What was tested
Real receipts, real conditions
  • Full end-to-end flow in real environments
  • MPC verification panel with mall managers
  • QA team consolidated findings; sales team and clients verified against expectations
What changed
Fixes & improvements
  • New error states for crumpled, faded, and partially visible receipts
  • Expanded manual verification options — managers needed more control
  • "Waiting for approval" copy clarified — users weren't sure if action was required
  • Technical bugs fixed quickly thanks to close QA collaboration, preventing many production issues
Post-launch iterations
New client requirements that made it to production
  • Some clients didn't want automatic verification at all and preferred to approve every scan manually — an opt-out from automation was added
  • Receipt upload (file) added as an option alongside camera scanning — a separate flow requested after initial launch
06 — Outcome

Shipped.

The scanner covers the full journey and was shipped as a standalone module for shopping centres adding spend-based loyalty rewards.

Team reaction on Slack after launch
My takeaway.

This project taught me how to design for multiple users, technical constraints, and tightly connected flows.
